findings.title: /mcp is exempt from the web auth layer; enabling HATCHDOOR_WEB_BEARER_TOKEN does not protect MCP read tools
affected: HATCHDOOR_MCP_ENABLED=true with no HATCHDOOR_MCP_BEARER_TOKEN and write disabled (read-only)
operator has set HATCHDOOR_WEB_BEARER_TOKEN believing the whole vault is locked down
non-browser client (curl) sending no Origin header, bypassing the origin allowlist
findings.description: In build_router the /mcp route is attached to the OPEN router (line 86), deliberately outside the require_web_token layer that guards every /api route (lines 46-82). Authentication for /mcp is a completely independent system in validate_mcp_request (src/mcp/config.rs:108-166): the MCP bearer token is only enforced when config.bearer_token is Some, and a read-only MCP deployment (write_enabled=false) is valid with bearer_token=None (validate() only requires a token for write mode). The origin allowlist is skipped entirely when no Origin header is present (config.rs:131 only runs when the header exists), so a headless client is unaffected. Net effect: a POST /mcp with method tools/call can invoke search_notes / get_note / get_tree and read the entire vault with no credentials, even though the operator set HATCHDOOR_WEB_BEARER_TOKEN.
findings.why: The two token systems (HATCHDOOR_WEB_BEARER_TOKEN vs HATCHDOOR_MCP_BEARER_TOKEN) are independent, and this is non-obvious. An operator who locks down the web UI for a public launch and turns on MCP for their own assistant, without also setting the MCP token, silently exposes full vault contents to anyone who can reach the port. MCP is off by default, which bounds the blast radius, but the coupling gap is a real data-exposure path for a public deployment.
findings.fixSketch: Require an MCP bearer token whenever MCP is enabled at all (make validate() reject enabled && bearer_token.is_none(), not just write mode), or document/enforce that /mcp inherits the web token when set. At minimum log a loud warning at startup when MCP is enabled without a bearer token.

findings.title: Attachment uploads are capped at axum's 2 MB default body limit while 10 MB is advertised/enforced downstream
affected: POST /api/attachment (upload_attachment_handler) with a file between 2 MB and max_attachment_bytes (default 10 MB)
any deployment relying on the advertised HATCHDOOR_MCP_MAX_ATTACHMENT_BYTES (default 10*1024*1024)
findings.description: build_router (src/main.rs:43-109) never sets DefaultBodyLimit, so axum 0.8's 2 MB default request-body limit applies to every extractor, including the Multipart extractor used by upload_attachment_handler. The handler then passes state.mcp_config.max_attachment_bytes (default 10*1024*1024, src/mcp/config.rs:82) into import_attachment_bytes (write_api.rs:186) as the real size ceiling, and that same 10 MB value is advertised to clients via the MCP get_attachment_import_config / tools output (src/mcp/tools.rs:52,396). A 3-10 MB image is rejected by the framework with a generic 413 before the handler code runs, so the 10 MB limit is never actually reachable over HTTP and the advertised value is misleading.
findings.why: Users are told 10 MB is allowed but real uploads fail at 2 MB with an opaque framework error (no ErrorResponse JSON body), which reads as a broken upload feature rather than a limit. The advertised-vs-actual mismatch is exactly the body-size concern flagged for launch.
findings.fixSketch: Apply an explicit DefaultBodyLimit sized from max_attachment_bytes (plus multipart overhead) to the attachment route, e.g. .layer(DefaultBodyLimit::max(max_attachment_bytes + slack)) on that route, and keep the JSON routes at a sane limit. Ensure the advertised max matches the enforced framework limit.

findings.title: Bearer token accepted as an access_token query parameter, exposing it in URLs and (at debug log level) request spans
affected: tower_http log level raised to debug (RUST_LOG), where DefaultMakeSpan records the full request URI
reverse proxies / browser history / Referer headers that capture full URLs
findings.description: request_is_authorized accepts the web token via the access_token query parameter (auth.rs:54-58) to support and download navigations that cannot set an Authorization header. Query strings are inherently logged and cached: the TraceLayer's DefaultMakeSpan (src/main.rs:104-106) records the request URI, which includes the query string, so raising tower_http to debug writes the token to logs. The default filter (tower_http=info, src/app_state.rs:109) suppresses that span, so this is not leaked by default, but the token still lands in browser history, proxy access logs, and potentially Referer headers for the affected asset/download URLs.
findings.why: Secrets in URLs are a recognized weakness; even with the default log level protecting against the span-logging path, the token is durably exposed in intermediaries the app does not control. Relevant to hardening before a public launch.
findings.fixSketch: Prefer a short-lived, scoped signed token (or a cookie set from the Authorization header) for asset/download URLs instead of the long-lived web bearer token, and explicitly redact the query string in the trace span.

findings.title: When HATCHDOOR_WEB_BEARER_TOKEN is unset, all mutating routes (write/delete/upload) are fully unauthenticated with only an info-level guardrail
affected: HOST=0.0.0.0 (or fronted without an auth proxy) exposing the port beyond localhost
findings.description: In build_router the protected router is only wrapped in the auth layer when web_bearer_token is Some (main.rs:76-82); when it is None the entire router - including POST /api/note, PUT/DELETE /api/note/{slug}, the rename/move/archive PATCH routes, and POST /api/attachment - is served with no authentication. The only guardrail against exposing this publicly is an info-level startup log (main.rs:122-127) emitted when host=="0.0.0.0" and no token is set, plus a warning string in the /api/write-capabilities body (write_api.rs:92-99). Nothing refuses to start or downgrades to read-only. Default host is 127.0.0.1 which bounds the risk, but an operator who sets HOST=0.0.0.0 and forgets the token silently exposes full unauthenticated create/delete of the vault.
findings.why: For a public launch, an insecure-by-default that allows anonymous deletion/overwrite of the entire vault, guarded only by an easily-missed info log, is a foot-gun. Content-hash checks prevent blind overwrites but not create/upload or hash-then-delete sequences.
findings.fixSketch: Refuse to bind a non-loopback host without a web token (hard error), or auto-disable frontend write routes when no token is configured, instead of only logging at info level.
